text_version.version: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (No. 34 of 2024), as published in the Government Gazette Acts Supplement No. 37 (22 Nov 2024; SSO status 'Published in Acts Supplement on 21 Nov 2024'); passed 15 Oct 2024, assented 8 Nov 2024, commencement 22 Jan 2025
text_version.note: Enacted Act (ss. 1-3: short title/commencement; amendments to the Parliamentary Elections Act 1954 incl. new s. 61MA; amendments to the Presidential Elections Act 1991 incl. new s. 42LA), replacing Bill No. 29/2024 as introduced (kept as .prev.txt.bak; old raw PDF kept as cache/raw/<id>.prev.pdf.bak). This is the amending Act as enacted, not the consolidated PEA/PrEA. Extracted with tools/extract_texts.py from the SSO HTML; the first ~60 lines are SSO page chrome (TOC, print controls). The bill's explanatory statement is not part of the Act.

territorial_scope.description: Applies to publication in Singapore of online election advertising during an election period, and to Returning Officer and candidate functions under the Parliamentary and Presidential Elections Acts.

evidence.quote: the person publishes, or causes to be published, in Singapore any content, or any thing containing content

summary.short: Amends Singapore's Parliamentary and Presidential Elections Acts to ban publishing online election advertising with realistic but false audio, visual or audiovisual depictions of candidates made with digitally generated or manipulated content during election periods. Commencement date: 22 January 2025.
summary.long: The Act amends the Parliamentary Elections Act 1954 and the Presidential Elections Act 1991 (sections 2 and 3). It creates an offence (new sections 61MA and 42LA) for a person who publishes, or causes to be published, in Singapore online election advertising during an election period that contains a representation of a candidate saying or doing something the candidate did not do, where the representation is realistic enough that some members of the public would likely believe it and was created wholly or partly with digitally generated or manipulated content. The offence requires that the person knows or ought reasonably to have known the content is election advertising. It is a defence to prove that the person did not know and had no reason to believe the candidate did not say or do the thing. Private communications, news published by authorised news agencies and other excluded circumstances are exempt. Offenders face a fine up to $1,000, imprisonment up to 12 months, or both. After a writ is issued, the Returning Officer must publish and maintain a public list of candidates who have deposited the required sum and consented to publication. Candidates may request Returning Officer directions in respect of these offences. Failure to comply with a direction is an offence, with a fine up to $1,000,000 for social media service providers and otherwise a fine up to $1,000 or imprisonment up to 12 months. Knowingly false or misleading requests are an illegal practice. The Act was passed on 15 October 2024 and assented on 8 November 2024; the document gives a date of commencement of 22 January 2025.

relations.note: Amends the Act by inserting s 28(1C) and s 61MA, replacing words in the Part 3 Division 3 heading, inserting and replacing references in s 61N, and amending s 61S(3).
Amends the Act by inserting s 10(2A) and s 42LA, replacing words in the Division 2A Subdivision (3) heading, inserting and replacing references in s 42M, and amending s 42R(3).

relations.target_text: election advertising regulations (referred to in s 61MA(4)(c) as inserted by s 2(c); parallel reference in s 42LA(4)(c) as inserted by s 3(c))
relations.note: The inserted exclusions allow publishing in other circumstances prescribed by the election advertising regulations. The regulations are not identified in this text.

evidence.quote: any publishing of content by electronic means in other circumstances prescribed by the election advertising regulations as excluded from subsection (1)

notes: The Act amends only the Parliamentary Elections Act 1954 and the Presidential Elections Act 1991; it names no enabling act, repeals or implemented instrument. Commencement: s 1 says the Act comes into operation on a date the Minister appoints by notification in the Gazette, but the document header states 'Date of Commencement: 22 January 2025', which does not appear in s 1 and should be checked against a commencement notice. The publication date is inconsistent in the document: the status line says 'Published in Acts Supplement on 21 Nov 2024' while the Gazette masthead reads 'Friday, November 22 [2024'. The Act's 'Illustrations' to ss 61MA and 42LA are part of the operative text as printed.

thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff changing scope, eligibility, exemption, obligation tier or prohibition was found. The amounts in the text (fines of $1,000 and $1,000,000, imprisonment of 12 months) are penalty maxima recorded under enforcement. Commencement is set by ministerial notification, which is an event rather than a threshold.
